I am Ahsan Mahmood, an AI-native full-stack developer in Lahore with 8+ years of hands-on experience. AI agents write most of my code now; I decide what they build, review it and confirm it works. That is one way to get software made. These are the other five, including the jobs where I would send you to them.

I can write all of this by hand, and for most of my career I did. I work through AI agents now because they produce code far faster than I can. I decide what gets built and how, I tell them, and I review what comes back. Nothing is finished until I have confirmed it is correct. What took me a month now takes a day or a week, and I would put the change at 10 to 100 times. That is my own statement from doing the work rather than a measurement, so read it beside the dates here.

None of these is the wrong answer. Each one fits some jobs better than I do, and its page says which. An agency — Choose it when the work needs several people at the same hour. An inexperienced developer — Choose it when the job is small and the mistakes are cheap. A vibe coder — Choose it when you want to test an idea on real people this week. A freelancer from a large marketplace — Choose it for a small job with a clear finish. Doing it in-house — Choose it when the software is the business and needs someone every day for years.

An agency sells you a team under one contract. I am one developer who directs AI agents. For some jobs the team is plainly the better buy. Choose it when the work needs several people at the same hour.
documents.s: Hiring an agency or hiring me — Ahsan Mahmood

documents.t: An agency is the better choice when the work needs several people at the same hour: a large build on a fixed date, brand and illustration alongside the code, or round-the-clock support with a rota behind it. I am one person, and I am not a designer. It is also right when you want one contract to cover design, development and support for years, with the agency deciding who does each part.

A team under one contract: usually an account manager, a designer, a few developers and someone checking the work. You talk to the account manager, and the account manager talks to the people building it. A good agency has a process and a bench. If a developer leaves or falls ill, somebody else picks the work up and you may never hear about it.

You talk to the person doing the work. The person who models the data also writes the security rules, packages the Android build and answers the store reviewer, so nothing gets lost between a brief and a developer. The team I direct is AI agents rather than staff. They write the code far faster than I can, and I decide what they build, review what comes back and run it before you hear about it. There is no handover between people for a detail to fall through. The handover assumes I am not available: full IP transfer, and documentation that matches the code.

documents.t: A marketplace gives you a long list of people and a way to hold the money until you approve. The difficulty is telling, before you have paid, which kind of person you have found. Choose it for a small job with a clear finish.
documents.s: A marketplace freelancer or me — Ahsan Mahmood

documents.t: For a small job with a clear finish, a marketplace is hard to beat: a bug fix, a landing page, one screen built from a design you already have. Its escrow and dispute process are also real protection, and a direct arrangement with me does not come with them. If that matters most to you, stay on the platform.

A search box, a long list of profiles, and bids that arrive quickly. You choose from ratings, a portfolio and a short message, and the platform holds the money until you approve the work. The person you get might be excellent. A rating tells you that earlier buyers were happy with earlier jobs, and those jobs may look nothing like yours.

You do not have to trust a rating. Everything I have built that can be shown is on this site with a link that opens it: 23 products are live today, and you can use them before you write to me. Scoping happens on a call, before any number. A fixed number attached to an unscoped brief is a number one of us is going to be unhappy about, and the call is where I say whether I am the right person. The cost of that is time up front. A call and a written scope are slower than accepting a bid, and for a small job they are not worth it.
My side of this rests on the products below. Each one opens, and each date comes from its commit history or my own project records.

documents.t: Your own team knows your business and stays. If the software is the business, that is where it belongs in the end. The question is what happens before that team exists. Choose it when the software is the business and needs someone every day for years.
documents.s: Building in-house or hiring me — Ahsan Mahmood

documents.t: If the software is the business and it will need someone every day for years, build the team. No outside developer should be the long-term answer for your core product. In-house is also right when the knowledge cannot leave the building, or when you already have engineers and a settled roadmap.

Your own employee or team: someone who knows the business, sits in your meetings and still remembers why a decision was made three years later. It is usually the slowest route to start, because you have to find them, hire them and keep them busy once the first release is out.

I fit the stretch before that: the first release, the codebase that needs rescuing, the product your team has no time to start. Taking over someone else's code usually begins with an audit and a prioritised roadmap. You get a product without a hiring round, and the handover assumes I am not available. You are not buying a codebase only I can read. If the project only runs while I am on it, I have not finished. And if the right answer turns out to be hiring a senior who works this way, I am open to remote roles too.

documents.t: A newer developer costs less and often works hard. What you are short of is someone who has already seen how this kind of project goes wrong. Choose it when the job is small and the mistakes are cheap.
documents.s: An inexperienced developer or me — Ahsan Mahmood

documents.t: This is the better choice when the job is small and the mistakes are cheap: a brochure site, an internal script, a prototype you will throw away. It is also right when you already have a senior who can review the work and you want to train someone. Paying me for that buys more than you need.

A lower rate and, often, real energy. Someone early in their career will usually take work a senior would turn down, and plenty of them learn quickly. You also become the senior. Someone has to decide the architecture, read the code and spot what will break in a year. If nobody does, it does not get done.

I have been shipping production software since January 2018, at five companies and then on my own. Much of that experience is a list of things I have already got wrong. The exam platform went down because a free-tier read quota ran out, and every list query I have written since has carried an explicit limit. Experience also decides what happens with AI agents. An agent writes whatever it is told, with the same confidence whether the idea is good or bad. Knowing which is which is the part of the job I kept for myself. And I can still write it by hand. When an agent goes the wrong way, I can see where, and I can take over rather than asking it to guess again.

documents.t: A vibe coder describes an app to an AI tool and ships what comes out, without an engineering background behind it. I use the same kind of tools, so speed is not what separates us. Choose it when you want to test an idea on real people this week.
documents.s: A vibe coder or me — Ahsan Mahmood

documents.t: For a demo, a landing page or an idea you want to try on real people this week, this is the right call. Nobody should pay a senior developer to find out whether anyone wants the thing. If it works, you will know what to build properly, and you will have spent very little to learn it.

Someone with no engineering background, or you yourself, describing an app to an AI tool and shipping what comes out. The first version can appear in an afternoon, and it can look finished. What you do not get is anyone who can tell you whether it is finished. The tool will say that it is.

The difference is what happens after the agent says it is done. I read the code, run the real flow as a real user, check the security rules and look at what the database allows. A demo and a product look the same until someone signs in with the wrong account, a quota runs out or the store reviewer writes back. A green build is not evidence that a feature works. The first two days of rebuilding this site, below, are the example I would point at: eight defects that the automated checks had passed. That review is the slow part, and it stays with me. Agents made the writing fast; they did not make the checking fast.
